sections.section_title: Introduction to One-Sided Laplace Transform Definition
sections.learning_goal: Define the one-sided Laplace transform as a causal-domain mapping from a time signal $x(t)$ to a complex-domain function $X(s)$ using the lower limit $0^-$ and the exponential kernel $e^{-st}$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual objects are required to establish the symbolic transform definition.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Introduce the one-sided transform definition and explicitly contrast it with two-sided transforms by stating when the $0^-$ lower limit is used for causal/signal-analysis work.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Set up $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty} x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$ for a simple causal signal such as $x(t)=u(t)$ and identify each component.
paragraph_plan: Introduce the motivation for using one-sided transforms in causal signal and system analysis and define the meaning of $s=\sigma + j\omega$.
State the formula $X(s)=\int_{0^-}^{\infty} x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$ and annotate the roles of $x(t)$, $e^{-st}$, and $dt$.
Explain why $0^-$, not 0, captures impulses/jumps at the origin and preserves causal initial conditions.
Give a compact comparison sentence between one-sided setup and bilateral setup to anchor the distinction.

sections.handoff_notes: Use this as the only pure tutorial block. No questions in this section. Keep pacing lightweight, then move immediately into worked examples in later sections.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that the one-sided transform is set as $\mathcal{L}_{+}\{x(t)\}=\int_{0^-}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$ and that for $x(t)=\delta(t)$, the integral collapses by sifting.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Compute $\mathcal{L}_{+}\{\delta(t)\}$ from the definition and simplify to $1$.
paragraph_plan: State the one-sided transform definition and highlight that the lower limit is $0^-$.
Define the impulse sifting identity used in transform work: $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(t)f(t)dt=f(0)$ and its one-sided analog when $0^-$ is used.
Set up the transform for $x(t)=\delta(t)$ as $\int_{0^-}^{\infty}\delta(t)e^{-st}dt$.
Apply the rule by replacing $\delta(t)\,e^{-st}$ with the sampled value at $t=0$, then simplify $e^{-s\cdot 0}$.
Conclude $\mathcal{L}_{+}\{\delta(t)\}=1$ and name the boundary role of $0^-$ for later shifted-impulse steps.

Finish with a short execution checklist: identify $T$, test the interval condition, then write the transform.
